facts.value: Treasury Management Strategy Outturn 2025/26. Report to Audit and Performance Committee, 30 June 2026, onward to Full Council by 30 September 2026 (regulatory requirement, para 1.2). Signed by Gerald Almeroth, Executive Director for Finance and Resources; report author Sophie Green, Treasury Manager (contact sgreen1@westminster.gov.uk, page 11 background papers block).

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy Outturn 2025/26 — Audit and Performance Committee, 30 June 2026

facts.note: Twelve-page outturn covering the full 2025/26 year, plus Appendix 1 (page 12) listing counterparty limits and exposures at 31/3/26. Report says the Council complied with all elements of the TMSS (para 1.5). Treasury operation is run by the Tri-Borough Treasury team (para 3.1).

facts.value: 31/3/26: Total Borrowing £569.0m; Total Cash Invested £306.3m; Net Cash Invested (£262.6m). Comparators 31/3/25: £572.7m borrowing / £463.4m investments / (£109.3m) net. Investment book down £157.1m year on year; borrowing down £3.7m.
facts.note: Para 3.2 states the net-cash position moved £153.3m year on year (from (£109.3m) to (£262.6m)) driven by continued use of internal borrowing to fund capital (paras 3.5, 3.14). Average investable balance across the year £643.6m (para 3.4).

facts.value: 31/3/26 breakdown (para 3.22, page 5): PWLB £113.6m (from £120.7m, −£7.0m); LOBO £40.0m (unchanged); Private Placement £386.4m (from £392.2m, −£5.8m); Amber MEEF/Abundance £28.9m (from £19.8m, +£9.1m). Total £569.0m. GF/HRA split (para 3.21): GF £430.3m (from £427.0m); HRA £138.6m (from £145.7m).
facts.note: PWLB is only 20.0% of the book, LOBOs 7.0%, Private Placements 67.9%, Amber MEEF/Abundance 5.1%. £9.1m of net new borrowing in year via the Amber MEEF/Abundance line — the only rising component. No new PWLB or LOBO borrowing. Para 3.24: council took no additional long-term borrowing in 2025/26 due to high cash holdings, so the £7m PWLB drop is amortisation/maturity and the £5.8m private placement drop is annuity/EIP repayment on the Phoenix and Rothesay tranches.

facts.value: Para 3.26–3.27, page 5: £400m of forward borrowing arranged in 2019/20 with insurance-company counterparties, £386.4m still outstanding at 31/3/26 at a weighted 2.579% average interest rate. Breakdown: Phoenix Group £37.5m initial / £12.8m outstanding at 2.706%, annuity, drawn 15/3/2022, maturing 15/3/2062; Barings LLC £150.0m / £150.0m at 1.970%, maturity, drawn 15/8/2022, maturing 15/8/2052; Phoenix Group £12.5m / £12.0m at 2.751%, annuity, drawn 15/3/2023, maturing 15/3/2063; Rothesay Life Plc £200.0m / £189.0m at 2.887%, equal instalment of principal, drawn 8/5/2023, maturing 8/5/2063.
facts.note: This is the distinctive feature of Westminster's book. Rates locked in 2019/20 for 30–40 year terms at 1.97%–2.89% — years before the October 2019 PWLB margin hike and years before the 2022 gilt sell-off. Explicit rationale (para 3.26): eliminating cost of carry, i.e., the difference between loan interest cost and rate of return on cash investments. Against today's PWLB CERTAINTY curve at notice 314/26 PM (as at 2026-08-14) of ~6.27%–6.46% at 25–50y, the £386.4m book at 2.579% carries in the order of 350–400 basis points of value below current comparable cost. Not something the paper computes; visible from the platform's daily curve.

facts.value: TIES EXACTLY. price_book.py 'WESTMINSTER CITY COUNCIL' --as-at 2026-03-31 returns 14 loans outstanding, principal £113,645,000, weighted rate 3.6016%, all MATURITY profile. Paper's para 3.22 table shows PWLB balance at 31/3/26 of £113.6m. Both sides agree to the pound.

source.title: price_book.py output vs paper para 3.22, page 5

facts.note: Paper prints only the PWLB total, not a PWLB-only weighted rate — its 2.87% overall rate (para 3.38) is for the whole £569m fixed book (dominated by 2.579% private placement). So the 3.60% weighted rate on our PWLB extract cannot be cross-checked to a printed number, but the balance and the composition (PWLB is 20% of the book, everything else is Private Placement / LOBO / Amber MEEF) match cleanly. PWLB spread across the curve: 1 loan £4m <12m at 3.73%; 1 loan £4m 1–2y at 3.81%; 4 loans £27.7m 2–5y at 3.40%; 5 loans £50m 5–10y at 3.52%; 1 loan £7.945m 10–25y at 3.43%; 2 loans £20m 25y+ at 4.10%. Break-cost curve at notice 314/26 PM shows a net DISCOUNT of £9.20m (8.1% of principal), all 14 loans below par — because PWLB certainty rates today (5.34% at 5y, 5.83% at 10y, 6.27% at 50y) sit above the loans' 3.4%–4.1% coupons. INDICATIVE ONLY; only the DMO can quote.

facts.value:
CFR − external borrowing − other long-term liabilities = internal borrowing.
• Using the paper's headline CFR (para 3.19 and summary table page 7): £1,338m − £569m − £286m = £483m internal borrowing. TIES to the paper's stated £483m under-borrowed position (para 3.20 and summary table).
• Using the detailed CFR reconciliation (page 8, total column): £1,748m closing CFR − £569m − £286m = £893m. DOES NOT TIE to the £483m headline.
The two CFR figures in the paper differ: £1,338m appears in both the summary indicator table (page 7) and paragraph 3.19; £1,748m appears as the total closing CFR in the detailed reconciliation on page 8 (GF £1,338m + HRA £410m). The headline figure is the GF-only column, not the total. Both identity calculations are internally consistent to the pound.

source.title: Paras 3.19–3.20 and summary indicator table, page 7; detailed CFR reconciliation, page 8

facts.note: Genuine internal inconsistency in the paper — the summary table quotes CFR £1,338m and treats it as the total ("Net debt vs CFR £483m" is calculated against total gross debt £855m), but the detailed reconciliation table on page 8 shows total closing CFR of £1,748m across GF (1,338) and HRA (410). Recorded here; NOT raised in the email — reads as fault-finding. The £483m under-borrowed figure is what the paper repeatedly quotes and is what a reader would take.

facts.value: Para 3.6 table, 31/3/26: Money Market Funds £74.3m at 3.83%; UK Banks £10.0m at 4.37%; Non-UK Banks £25.0m at 4.16%; Local Authorities £197.0m at 4.46%; Total £306.3m at weighted 4.28%. Comparators 31/3/25: MMF £33.4m at 4.55%; UK £50.0m at 4.75%; Non-UK £50.0m at 4.78%; LA £330.0m at 5.34%; Total £463.4m at 5.16%. Every yield down between 60 and 90 basis points on Bank Rate cuts through the year (May, August, December, all 25bp — para 3.7).
facts.note: £197m at 4.46% to other councils is a very large LA lender position — Westminster is on the sell side of the inter-authority market at scale. Appendix 1 (page 12) names the counterparties: Doncaster (2 loans, £40m total at 4.25%), Dundee City (3 loans, £40m at 4.50%–4.90%), North Lanarkshire (6 loans, £50m at 4.05%–4.25%), Stockton-on-Tees (£12m at 4.25%), Surrey County Council (£20m at 4.10% and £10m at 7.50%), Telford and Wrekin (3 loans, £25m at 4.25%–4.30%). Total across the list is £197m. That's the LA row exactly.

facts.value: Para 3.11 table: 2025/26 Budget £27,983k, Actual £29,702k, Variance +£1,719k (favourable). Para 3.11 text conflicts with the table, stating budgeted investment return was £41.5m against actual £29.7m for a £11.8m under-budget outcome.
facts.note: Second internal inconsistency in the paper — table header labels the year '2024/25' but the surrounding paragraph is discussing 2025/26. The £27,983k budget in the table does not match the £41.5m budget quoted in the paragraph text. Table also has a stray '2024/25' year header. Recorded; NOT raised. Para 3.13 flags that treasury interest allocation differs from the council-wide revenue outturn report (Westminster Builds interest, Real Lettings Property Fund accruals allocated to other budgets).

facts.value: Summary table page 7, 2025/26 actual vs forecast: Capital expenditure £282m (forecast £579m); CFR £1,338m (forecast £1,594m); Net debt vs CFR £483m under-borrowed (forecast £1,035m); External borrowing £569m; Other Long-Term Liabilities £286m; Gross Debt £855m; Authorised Limit for External Debt £1,641m; Operational Boundary £605m — actual gross debt £855m EXCEEDED (para 3.31). Working Capital Balance £0m. Non-specified investment limit (>364d) £450m — actual £0m (para 3.42). Ratio of financing costs to revenue: GF 12.20% (limit 12.55%); HRA 30.33% (limit 58.42%). Maturity profile actual: 3% <12m (limit 40%), 2% 12–24m (limit 35%), 9% 24m–5y (limit 35%), 16% 5–10y (limit 50%), 70% 10y+ (lower limit 35%).

source.title: Summary indicator table, page 7; maturity structure para 3.36, page 6

facts.note: Operational Boundary breach explained by the A2Dominion lease transaction commencing April 2025 after the TMSS was set in February 2025 — para 3.31–3.32. Council remained comfortably within the £1,641m Authorised Limit. GF financing-cost ratio at 12.20% actual sits 35 basis points below its 12.55% limit — narrowest headroom in the summary table. Maturity profile is heavily long: 70% of borrowing sits 10 years and above, driven by the £386.4m private placement book maturing 2052–2063. Only 3% (about £17m of £569m) reprices in under 12 months.

facts.value: Para 3.38, page 6: 'The average rate on the fixed interest borrowing is 2.87% with an average redemption period of 19 years. This reflects the historical legacy of borrowing taken when rates were lower than current comparable PWLB interest rates.' The paper adds: 'Officers have considered loan refinancing but premia for premature redemptions are prohibitively high, making this option poor value for money.'
facts.note: The 2.87% whole-book rate is dominated by the £386.4m of private placements at 2.579% (68% of the book). PWLB piece at ~3.60% is a smaller weight. LOBO piece at £40m and Amber MEEF at £28.9m sit inside the average too. Premature-repayment premia — for the private placements, yes, they would be very high given today's 30–50y curve at 6.27%–6.46% CERTAINTY, versus their 1.97%–2.89% coupons. For the £113.6m PWLB piece specifically, today's DMO curve puts the book at a discount (14 of 14 below par, net £9.2m under principal), because their PWLB coupons (3.4%–4.1%) sit below today's PWLB replacement rates. So the para 3.38 statement is correct for the whole book but not for the PWLB piece considered alone. NOT the argument for the email.

facts.value: Para 3.39, page 6: £40.0m of Lender Option Borrower Option loans, described as up to 60-year term with periodic rate re-pricing. Paper states rates were 'comparable with loans for similar durations provided by the PWLB'. Paper acknowledges refinancing risk from lender option to redeem, and notes some banks offering premature repayment or conversion to fixed-term loans with officers 'alert to such opportunities as they arise'.
facts.note: Paper does NOT publish: LOBO lender name(s), individual loan sizes, next call date(s), current fixed rate(s). All would be needed to slot Westminster into the cross-council LOBO pattern (Kent/Tameside/Newcastle/Bath & NE Somerset/Wolverhampton/Staffordshire/Harrow etc). The council is a specifically-attentive holder — 'alert to such opportunities as they arise' is the strongest LOBO-conversion signal we have seen in the batch. Coverage gap on our side: LOBO stack is not in the PWLB file. NOT raised in the email as a comparative statement — we would be inviting them to fill our gap.

facts.value: Section 4, pages 8–10 (paper's own narrative): UK CPI 3.5% start of year, peaked 3.8% July–Sept 2025, dipped to 3.0% Jan/Feb 2026, core 3.2% Feb. Bank Rate cuts of 0.25% in May, August, December 2025 taking the headline rate 4.50% → 3.75%. Rate at 3.75% at report date; March MPC vote 9-0 to hold, moderately hawkish tone. 10-year gilt yield 4.23% low late-Feb, spiked to 5.00% on Middle East conflict, ended quarter 4.92% with ~65bp of hikes priced in over the coming year. Gilt yields materially higher in March 2026 than earlier in the year.
facts.note: Paper's rate view (3.75% held through 2026, hike risk if inflation picks up) tracks the paper's own year-end market view. Consistent with Arlingclose-style narrative on other August reports, though the paper does not name a treasury adviser.

internal_holdings.note: For internal record only — nothing here goes into the email beyond what the paper prints or what the reconciliation permits.
internal_holdings.cfr_headline_vs_detailed_table: Genuine inconsistency: summary indicator table (page 7) shows CFR £1,338m and Net debt vs CFR £483m under-borrowed, using total gross debt £855m; but the detailed CFR reconciliation on page 8 shows total closing CFR of £1,748m (GF £1,338m + HRA £410m). The '£1,338m CFR' in the headline is the GF-only column. If the detailed table's £1,748m total is the correct answer, the under-borrowed position would be £893m, not £483m. Not raised — the paper's own working repeatedly quotes £483m and reads as self-consistent to any reader who does not open the detailed reconciliation. Fault-finding on this would be off-brand for a first contact.
internal_holdings.mmf_direction_error_para_3_15: Para 3.15 states 'the Council maintained lower balances in Money Market Funds at year end (£33 million compared with £74 million the previous year)'. The direction is reversed against the para 3.6 table, which shows MMF £33.4m at 31/3/25 rising to £74.3m at 31/3/26 — MMF actually went UP year on year, not down. The narrative sentence has swapped the years. Not raised.
internal_holdings.investment_income_table_para_3_11: Para 3.11 text says '£41.5m budget vs £29.7m actual, £11.8m under budget'. The accompanying table shows Budget £27,983k / Actual £29,702k / Variance +£1,719k, with a stray '2024/25' year header. Table and text describe two different budget baselines and go in opposite directions on variance. Not raised.
internal_holdings.pwlb_discount_finding: PWLB piece at 3.60% weighted vs today's PWLB certainty curve (5.34% at 5y through 6.46% at 25y) prices as a £9.2m net discount, 8.1% of principal. That is genuinely at odds with para 3.38's statement that 'premia for premature redemptions are prohibitively high' — but para 3.38 is about the whole book, dominated by 2.579% private placements where premia truly would be prohibitive. Raising the PWLB-only discount reads as 'you could repay these cheaply' which is a) advice, b) misleading without replacement-cost modelling, and c) contradicts the council's evident preference to hold long. Not raised.
internal_holdings.gf_financing_cost_ratio_headroom: GF ratio 12.20% actual against 12.55% limit — 35bp of headroom, tightest in the indicator table. Considered as a hook; discarded because commenting reads as 'you're near your limit' which is advice-adjacent for a well-managed council that set both the limit and the actual.
internal_holdings.surrey_7_5_percent_deposit: Appendix 1 lists 'Surrey County Council 10.0 at 7.50%' alongside 'Surrey County Council 20.0 at 4.10%'. The 7.50% is 340bp above the other Surrey line and about 300bp above the top of the other LA rates in the same block (max 4.90%). It is an outlier by a large margin; may be a very short distressed line, or a table entry error. Not raised — commenting on another council's borrowing rate that a third council disclosed reads badly and we have no basis to say which reading is right.
internal_holdings.operational_boundary_breach_a2dominion: Para 3.31–3.32 explains the Operational Boundary was exceeded by the A2Dominion lease. Not raised as a finding — the paper explains it clearly and the council remained within the Authorised Limit. Nothing to add.
internal_holdings.no_named_treasury_adviser: Paper's economic commentary in section 4 reads like standard adviser copy (Bank Rate path, gilt-yield narrative, MPC vote tone) but the paper does not name an adviser. Recorded; irrelevant to the email.
internal_holdings.hooks_considered_ranked: 1) £400m of private placements at 2.579% locked in 2019/20 with insurers, and what that value looks like against today's 30–50y curve — LEAD. Distinctive across the 77 councils read. 2) Loan-book tie on the PWLB piece — cross-check paragraph to establish credibility. 3) Cost-of-carry framing from para 3.26 — specialist language worth quoting back. 4) Maturity profile 70% at 10y+ / 3% at <12m — the shape of a book that already did the terming-out work. 5) £197m of LA lending / Westminster as a net LA lender — considered, kept as flavour only. 6) LOBO — kept out; too much missing to say anything comparative. 7) GF financing-cost headroom — advice-adjacent, cut. 8) CFR inconsistency — internal only. 9) MMF direction / investment income table errors — internal only.

summary.text:
Westminster's Treasury Management Strategy Outturn 2025/26 to Audit and Performance Committee on 30 June 2026, onward to Full Council by 30 September (regulatory requirement, para 1.2). Report by Gerald Almeroth (Executive Director for Finance and Resources); author Sophie Green, Treasury Manager, whose address is printed in the background papers block on page 11. Council complied with all elements of the TMSS.

PWLB loan-book reconciliation: ties exactly. Our extract shows 14 PWLB loans at £113,645,000 outstanding at 31 March 2026, weighted 3.6016%; the paper's para 3.22 shows PWLB of £113.6m. To the pound. PWLB is only 20% of Westminster's book — the paper does not publish a PWLB-only weighted rate for direct comparison, but the balance and composition match cleanly.

The distinctive feature of Westminster's book is the £386.4m of private placements at 2.579% average. Arranged in 2019/20 as forward loans totalling £400m (paras 3.24–3.27), drawn 2022/23 for 30–40 year terms with Barings (£150m at 1.970%, maturity to 2052), Rothesay Life (£200m at 2.887%, EIP to 2063), and Phoenix Group (two annuity tranches totalling £50m at 2.706%/2.751% to 2062/2063). Against today's PWLB certainty curve at notice 314/26 PM (5.83% at 10y, 6.38% at 20y, 6.46% at 25y, 6.27% at 50y), the £386.4m carries in the order of 350–400 basis points of value below current comparable cost. That is by far the strongest treasury-execution story across the 77 councils we have read.

Balance-sheet identity ties on the headline figures. Paper's CFR £1,338m − external borrowing £569m − Other Long-Term Liabilities £286m = £483m internal borrowing, which matches the paper's stated £483m under-borrowed position (para 3.20 and summary table page 7). But the detailed CFR reconciliation on page 8 shows total closing CFR of £1,748m (GF £1,338m + HRA £410m), meaning the £1,338m headline figure is the GF-only column. If total CFR £1,748m were used, internal borrowing would be £893m rather than £483m. Recorded in the checks and internal blocks; NOT raised — reads as fault-finding on an otherwise clean paper.

Book is very long by design. Paper's own maturity profile (para 3.36): 70% of borrowing at 10 years and above (lower limit 35%); only 3% under 12 months (upper limit 40%). Average redemption period 19 years, whole-book rate 2.87% (para 3.38). The 70% long bucket is driven by the private placement stack all maturing 2052–2063. Refinancing risk in the next few years is not the story here.

Westminster is a net LA lender at scale. Appendix 1 (page 12) lists £197m out to six councils — Doncaster, Dundee, North Lanarkshire, Stockton-on-Tees, Surrey, Telford and Wrekin — at 4.05%–7.50% (that last a Surrey line, 340bp above its other Surrey line at 4.10% — flagged internally only, not raised). Total LA lending row of £197m at 4.46% weighted matches the para 3.6 investment table exactly. This is a large sell-side position in the inter-authority market.

Coverage gaps and non-hooks. LOBO: £40m held, paper does not publish lender, call date, or rate — cannot slot Westminster into the cross-council LOBO pattern. Amber MEEF/Abundance line rose from £19.8m to £28.9m — new borrowing in year, but non-PWLB and not something we can price. Two internal inconsistencies in the paper (the CFR headline vs detailed table split, and para 3.15's reversed year-on-year direction for MMF balances) both recorded internal-only.

Contact. Sophie Green, Treasury Manager, sgreen1@westminster.gov.uk — explicitly the report's contact for queries (page 11). Direct, no guessing. Draft goes to the 'ready to send' state with a mid-September send-by ahead of the Full Council item.

Draft. Leads with the loan-book tie, then the private-placement story quoted back at today's curve, then the paper's own cost-of-carry framing (para 3.26) which reads as specialist language worth acknowledging, then the shape of the book. About 620 words body.

checks.loan_book_reconciliation: TIES to the pound on the balance. 14 PWLB loans / £113,645,000 at 31/3/26 (price_book.py output) against the paper's £113.6m PWLB line in para 3.22 (page 5). PWLB-only weighted rate not printed in the paper for direct rate-to-rate comparison; whole-book rate 2.87% at para 3.38 is dominated by the 2.579% private placement piece, so a 3.60% PWLB weighted is consistent with the 2.87% blend.
checks.balance_sheet_identity: TIES on the paper's headline figures: £1,338m CFR − £569m external borrowing − £286m Other Long-Term Liabilities = £483m internal borrowing, matching the paper's stated £483m under-borrowed position at paras 3.19–3.20 and the summary table on page 7. The detailed CFR reconciliation on page 8 shows total closing CFR of £1,748m (GF 1,338 + HRA 410), which would give £893m internal — recorded in the checks record as an internal inconsistency in the paper, NOT raised in the email.
checks.figures_in_email_all_page_anchored: PWLB £113.6m and loan count / weighted rate — para 3.22 table (page 5) and price_book.py output. Whole-book average rate 2.87%, average life 19 years — para 3.38 (page 6). Private placement counterparties, initial amounts, outstanding balances, rates, dates, profile — para 3.27 table (page 5). Weighted 2.579% — para 3.27 table 'Average interest rate' row. Cost-of-carry framing — para 3.26 (page 5). Maturity profile 70% >10y / 3% <12m — para 3.36 table (page 6). External borrowing £569m — para 3.19 and para 3.22 (page 5). CFR £1,338m and £483m under-borrowed — para 3.19, 3.20 and summary table (page 7). LA lending £197m at 4.46% — para 3.6 table (page 3) and Appendix 1 (page 12). Bank Rate 3.75% — para 3.7 (page 3) and para 4.2 (page 9), matches PWLBtoday market data. 10y gilt 4.92% at end March — para 4.5 (page 10). Today's PWLB CERTAINTY curve at notice 314/26 PM — PWLBtoday market data as at 2026-08-14. July sector activity £368m / 33 loans / 19 borrowers / 5.02% — PWLBtoday July aggregate.
checks.certainty_rates_only: All PWLB rates in the email are CERTAINTY (standard less 20bp). Explicit statement in the body.
checks.break_costs_disclaimer: Email does not quote a break-cost figure. If mentioned as a reference to the /loan-analysis page, phrased as 'we price the book' with the standard 'only the DMO can quote' caveat. No specific settlement figure quoted for Westminster.
checks.no_advice: Email does not tell the Council to reprice, to switch counterparty, to term out differently, or to do anything else. It quotes the paper back, compares to public curve, and points at pages.
checks.no_recommendation_on_lobo: £40m LOBO acknowledged but no advice to convert or hold — paper's own 'alert to such opportunities' is quoted back rather than recommended. Coverage gap on our side (no LOBO stack in PWLB file) is not solicited as a fill-in from the Council.
checks.no_recommendation_on_la_lending: £197m LA lending discussed as flavour and as connection to the pwlb-activity page; no comment on the Surrey 7.50% outlier — recorded internal only.
checks.coverage_gap_pwlb_only: Email is explicit that we hold PWLB only and that the £113.6m PWLB is 20% of the £569m book; the private placement, LOBO and Amber MEEF pieces are not in our file. Standard 'we hold PWLB only' disclosure without inviting correction.
checks.no_national_ranking: 'Distinctive across the 77 councils we have read' — scoped, not implied as national. No claims about sector-wide ranking.
checks.cfr_inconsistency_not_raised: GF-vs-total CFR inconsistency in the paper (page 7 headline vs page 8 detailed table) is recorded in the checks record and internal_holdings but NOT surfaced in the email. Reads as fault-finding on an otherwise well-executed report.
checks.mmf_direction_error_not_raised: Para 3.15's reversed year-on-year direction for MMF balances (says 'lower' when the table shows the balance rose from £33m to £74m) recorded internal only, not raised.
checks.investment_income_table_error_not_raised: Para 3.11 text/table mismatch (£41.5m budget in text, £27,983k in table) recorded internal only, not raised.
checks.pwlb_discount_not_raised: PWLB break-cost curve shows the 14 PWLB loans at a £9.2m net discount to par. Directly repayable at that discount, but para 3.38's 'premia prohibitively high' statement is about the whole book (dominated by 1.97%–2.89% private placement) where premia would be huge. Not raised — reads as advice and misleads without replacement-cost modelling.

officer.body:
Dear Sophie,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on your Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 ahead of it reaching Full Council by the end of September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is compact and well-executed and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A quick cross-check first. We hold 14 PWLB loans for the Council totalling £113,645,000 at 31 March 2026, against the £113.6m in your para 3.22 table. To the pound. Your paper doesn't print a PWLB-only weighted rate — the 2.87% at para 3.38 is the whole £569m fixed book — but the balance and composition match cleanly.

The part of the paper that's genuinely distinctive is your para 3.27 table. Of the 77 councils we've read, Westminster is the only book we've come across built around £400m of forward-placement debt with insurers. Barings at 1.970% out to 2052, Rothesay at 2.887% out to 2063, and Phoenix at 2.706% and 2.751% out to 2062 and 2063 — weighted 2.579% across the £386.4m still outstanding. Against today's PWLB certainty curve at notice 314/26 PM (5.83% at 10 years, 6.38% at 20 years, 6.27% at 50 years), that's on the order of 350 to 400 basis points of value locked in below current comparable cost. Your para 3.26 framing — that these loans 'eliminated the cost of carry' between borrowing rate and cash return — is the specialist reading of what happened, and one that reads the same way six years later. The value was in the year the trades went on and it compounds every year they stay in the ground. It's also why your maturity profile prints 70% at 10 years and above against a 35% lower limit, and only 3% under 12 months — refinancing risk isn't the story here in the way it is for most councils we read.

Where the interesting question does sit is the other side of the balance sheet. £197m out to six other councils at a weighted 4.46% at 31 March, against Bank Rate 3.75% and yields off up to 90 basis points across your investment categories through the year (your para 3.6 versus 31 March 2025) — Westminster's Appendix 1 is one of the fuller sell-side snapshots we've seen of the inter-authority market, and it's the market nobody publishes. Every council sees its own trades and none sees the distribution. Our monthly page at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity aggregates what authorities are actually paying for shorter-dated money; July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers, average 5.02%.

On the PWLB side, pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis prices the 14 loans against the DMO's premature repayment curve daily. Standard caveats: we hold PWLB only (LOBO, private placement and Amber MEEF aren't in our file), we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a settlement figure. The rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds for the day's curve.

On training, four fit the shape of your book. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator, for the PWLB piece. Non-PWLB debt: private placement and insurance-company lending, which is the market where the 2019/20 trades sit. LOBO loans, for the £40m at para 3.39 and the 'alert to opportunities' language. And the Liability benchmark pathway is worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are open to the whole team.

And if any of it turns out to be useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
